extracted.intended_audience: public relations students, journalism educators, and entry-level PR job seekers
extracted.subtask_description: Survey-based summary of what San Francisco Bay Area public relations employers (circa 1977) seek in entry-level hires, covering preferred education and coursework, skills and personal traits, experience, recruitment methods, testing practices, affirmative action attitudes, and salary expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grapevine referrals (how jobs are filled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most job vacancies are filled by the 'grapevine' process — employers circulate openings among themselves or announce positions at PRSA or Round Table meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 65% of respondents cited grapevine referrals as the most frequent method. Aspiring job seekers should develop professional contacts and participate in professional organizations (e.g., attend PRSA chapter meetings). Advertisements reach many applicants and have limited utility; employers seldom recruit on campus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resumes received (applicant screening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of resumes received is a common method of identifying applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resumes are the second-most frequent method for finding applicants. Sending resumes to multiple employers has merit, but ads generate large applicant pools (~300/app) making limited-experience graduates disadvantaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal transfer or promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Filling vacancies by promoting or transferring internal staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About 20% reported filling positions by internal transfer or promotion; employers consider internal mobility a significant source of hires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and media used to announce openings
rubrics_metrics.description: When advertisements are used, they appear in publications such as the Wall Street Journal, metropolitan newspapers, and trade journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ads are infrequent (1% in some categories) and generate many applicants; trade publications (Public Relations Journal, Advertising Age, regional trades) are also used sometimes. Employment agencies are rarely used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruiting visits to campuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether employers make on-campus recruiting visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations employers generally do not conduct recruiting visits to campuses; campus recruitment is uncommon in this field per survey respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-year undergraduate degree requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A bachelor's (four-year) degree is regarded as the prerequisite for entry-level public relations jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 77% of respondents regarded a four-year undergraduate degree as necessary. A minority reported no educational minimum or some college; only 2% indicated a master's degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred college coursework
rubrics_metrics.description: Course areas employers prefer applicants to have completed: news/feature writing, principles of public relations, publicity, social sciences, finance/accounting, business administration, economics, editing/layout, speech communication, radio-television, advertising, photography, marketing, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business courses (finance, accounting, management) ranked high — often seen as more important than editing, broadcasting, advertising, or photography. Employers stress understanding business/financial statements for annual reports. Large firms may value specialized backgrounds (environmental science, geography, computer programming, foreign languages) depending on client needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write well and knowledge of journalistic style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing skills were emphasized 'a lot' by 99% of respondents. Employers often assess writing via writing/editing tests or by reviewing samples of applicants' work; one respondent: 'Writing ability and knowledge of journalistic style is the overwhelming criteria.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral communication and public speaking skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speaking ability received substantial weight (e.g., cited among top 'yardsticks'); public relations employers placed more emphasis on speaking ability (65%) than newspaper employers in a comparison study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant's attitude toward work and the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitude was among the yardsticks with 70% or more listing it as 'a lot' of consideration. Employers often evaluate attitude informally during interviews; it's a key subjective measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived potential for future development and advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth potential was highly weighted by employers (70%+ rated it 'a lot'); it's considered along with subjective traits and can influence hiring despite being hard to measure objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality
rubrics_metrics.description: General personality fit with the organization/team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personality is a major hiring yardstick (70%+ 'a lot'). Employers assess personality through interviews and informal impressions; this contributes to subjective hiring decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant drive and desire for advancement and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition was among the top-rated 'yardsticks' (70%+). Employers value candidates who show career focus and motivation; this can be assessed via interview responses and past activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poise
rubrics_metrics.description: Composure, professionalism, and presentational confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poise received high emphasis (70%+). Employers regard poise as important especially for client-facing roles; it's evaluated in interviews and simulated situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to work well with others and be a team player.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperativeness was frequently given 'a lot' of weight and is one of several interpersonal traits employers prioritize alongside attitude and personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical appearance and professional presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearance was emphasized more by PR employers (62% 'a lot') than by newsroom employers. The report notes a risk that glamour may sometimes be favored over substantive skills (e.g., 'a woman in public relations can be hired on the basis of glamour instead of grammar').

rubrics_metrics.name: Related part-time or full-time work experience in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior paid or volunteer work in public relations or related roles during college.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related work experience is an important 'yardstick' and is considered more positively than unrelated part-time work. Employers value demonstrated field experience when evaluating applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience on a newspaper or publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical experience on newspapers (professional or student publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience on a newspaper was a valued criterion (though PR employers placed somewhat less emphasis on newspaper experience than newspaper employers did). Experience on publications demonstrates writing and editorial skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of mass media
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding of media operations and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of mass media was a frequently-weighted yardstick; PR employers rated this higher than newspaper employers in a comparative study, indicating its relevance for press relations and media strategy work.

rubrics_metrics.name: References and letters of recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional references, letters of recommendation, and endorsements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References were among the considerations rated 'a lot' by employers. Grapevine referrals and recommendations from practitioners often carry strong weight in hiring decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening tests — overall use
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which employers use formal pre-employment testing or screening devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalized testing is not the rule: 46% reported not using any testing devices; only 12% gave 'a lot' of weight to testing results. Many employers prefer interviews and work-sample review over standardized tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of pre-employment tests used
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific tests employed when testing is used: writing/editing tests, spelling/grammar tests, psychological tests, organizational/case-problem tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing and editing tests are the most prevalent among those who test; 25% use spelling/grammar tests, 15% use psychological tests, and fewer use organizational-capacity (case problem) tests. Many employers instead review samples of applicants' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grade point average (GPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant's academic grades and GPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GPA appears on the list of items considered (Table 4) but did not rank as highly as writing ability, attitude, or work experience; it's considered among multiple factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative action — female candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer weighting of sex (female) when reviewing candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 69% indicated no preference on the basis of sex; 2% said more likely to hire a female if as qualified as a male; some employers' decisions depended on the job or client (e.g., food accounts sometimes favor women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative action — minority candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer weighting of race/ethnicity when reviewing candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 62% indicated no preference on the basis of race; 26% were more likely to hire a minority if equally qualified as a white applicant; a small number indicated they might hire a minority even if not quite as qualified. Federal-contract industries showed more active affirmative action hiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary expectations and progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical starting and five-year salary ranges reported by employers and factors influencing pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry-level salaries were reported most frequently between $7,500 and $10,500 annually; after five years, $14,000–$20,000 was typical depending on competence and promotions. Salary depends on account size/profitability and willingness to relocate for advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on intuition and subjective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers often hire based on hunches and subjective impressions rather than standardized metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study concludes many hiring criteria (personality, attitude, ambition, poise, cooperativeness) are subjective and lack standardized measurement, leading to hiring by intuition. This can disadvantage qualified candidates without 'connections' to the grapevine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to develop professional contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice for job seekers to build networks and tap the grapevine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many vacancies circulate via practitioner networks, aspiring PR job seekers should develop professional contacts while in college — attend PRSA meetings, join professional organizations, and cultivate relationships with practitioners to access unadvertised job leads.
